intro: You can get an AI first draft of marketing copy in about a minute. Getting it to sound like your brand takes a voice card, a few real samples, and a human edit before anything goes live. This page covers what off-brand copy costs you, why AI drifts away from your voice, and fixes you can use on a Mac today.
tldr: An AI first draft is fast. A draft in your brand voice needs a voice card and real samples.
Ahrefs' 2026 survey found that 66% of marketers trust AI content only after a human reviews it.
Models drift toward a typical, generic voice, and AI-assisted writing tends to look more alike across writers.
Start free: a one-page voice card, three to five real samples, and a banned words list.
Lazur drafts and types text and keeps snippets. It cannot know your voice without the samples you give it.

blocks.text: What off-brand AI copy costs you

Most of the cost is hidden. The draft arrives fast, so it feels like a win. Then you spend the saved time rewriting sentences that could have come from any company. Ahrefs' 2026 survey of 301 respondents found that 280 of them, or 93%, use AI for content creation. Two-thirds said they trust AI-generated content only if a human reviews it first.

Those numbers describe a team that expects a review step. Only 2.7% of respondents trust AI content with no review at all. If your draft ships without a check, you are in a small group, and you are the one who answers for the tone.

Readers notice too. In the same survey, 56% of AI users say human-written content is better quality than their AI content, and 23% say it is way better. The gap is not only about grammar. It is about the feeling that a real person wrote the post.

blocks.text: Time is the other cost. CMI's February 2026 survey of 644 full-time marketers found that 59% say their workload feels overwhelming, and 76% say they do the work of more than one job. That survey measures general workload, not AI-specific work. Still, a draft that needs heavy rewriting adds work to a week that already has no room.
Why AI copy drifts away from your voice

A language model writes from patterns in a large amount of text. Without strong signals, it returns the most typical version of a post. That version is smooth, polite, and easy to forget. Your brand voice lives in details the model cannot see, such as how you open, which words you avoid, and how bluntly you say things.

Padmakumar and He (arXiv 2309.05196) tested writing with language models. Writing with InstructGPT significantly reduced diversity in the text, and different authors' writing became more similar. The parts the writers contributed stayed unaffected. The sameness came from the model's own sentences, not from the people. Those models date from 2023, so test current tools on your own samples.

Jakesch and colleagues ran a CHI 2023 study with 1,506 participants (arXiv 2302.00560). Participants wrote with an assistant set up to argue that social media was good or bad. The assistant's opinions shifted the opinions in participants' writing and their later attitudes. Cornell's write-up says people using the biased assistant were twice as likely to write a paragraph agreeing with it. For marketers, a model's built-in framing can leak into your message.

Doshi and Hauser's dataset covers 293 participants who wrote short stories with and without generative AI ideas. The authors describe AI-enabled stories as more similar to each other than stories by humans alone. If five people on your team use the same prompt, expect five posts that sound alike.
Why a voice guide alone often falls short

Wang and colleagues (arXiv 2509.14543) tested whether language models can imitate an individual's writing style from a few samples. They ran more than 40,000 generations per model and used writing from more than 400 real authors. Models approximated styles in structured formats like news and email. They struggled with nuanced, informal writing in blogs and forums. Many brand voices are informal, so expect that gap.

A voice card made of adjectives still helps, but it is weak on its own. Friendly, bold, and smart describes almost any company. Samples carry more signal. A banned words list carries even more, because it removes the defaults the model reaches for first.
Fixes you can use today, without buying anything

Each fix below uses tools you already have, such as Google Docs, a notes app, and Writing Tools on a Mac where Apple Intelligence is available. None needs a new subscription. Start with the first two, because they solve most of the drift. The rest tighten the result.
Write a one-page voice card

Keep the card to one page in a Google Doc. Name five traits and give a counter-example for each. For example, write: Plain, not cute. Say 'ships Tuesday,' not 'get ready to be excited about Tuesday.' Add sentence rhythm, your usual opener and closer, words you use, words you avoid, and how you handle numbers and claims. Pin the link where your team drafts.
Paste three to five real samples

Anthropic's prompting guide says examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer tone. It suggests three to five examples for best results, and it recommends examples that are relevant and diverse. Pick samples from work you are proud of. Mix formats, such as an email, a short social post, and a help article. Skip weak samples, because the model copies flaws as easily as strengths.
Draft in steps, not in one prompt

Ask for three openers first. Pick one, then ask for the body. Then ask for an edit against your voice card, and ask the model to name the two rules it broke. Small steps show you where drift starts. One giant prompt hides it in the middle of a long draft.
Use Writing Tools for a second pass, not the first

Select the text in any app, Control-click the selection, and choose Show Writing Tools. Apple's guide lists Rewrite with Friendly, Professional, or Concise, plus Proofread and Summarize. Those rewrites move text toward a general tone. Use them to tighten a paragraph you already wrote in your voice, not to write it from scratch. Compose uses the ChatGPT extension and is only available where ChatGPT is. Apple Intelligence is not available in every language or region, and usage limits may apply.
Keep a banned words list and a claims list

Write down the hype words your readers roll their eyes at, and the phrases your legal or product team never allows. Search each draft against that list before you read it. Then add the words you deleted during edits. Every deleted word marks a default the model reaches for.
A worked example: one launch email, start to finish

Say you launch a reporting tab in your app. You have a voice card, four past emails, and a launch note from product. Open the Google Doc with the card and samples. Ask for three subject lines in your voice, then pick one. Ask for a body in three short paragraphs, each with one concrete detail from the product note.

A weak first draft often reads like this: 'We are thrilled to announce a powerful new way to see your data.' The fix is specific: 'The new reporting tab shows last week's numbers on one screen. No more copying rows into a sheet on Monday morning.' You removed the empty adjective. You added a fact a reader can check.

Then run the checklist. Search for banned words. Mark every number and confirm it against the product note. Read the email aloud once. Ask one colleague which lines sound like you. Log how many minutes the edit took, so you can compare it with your usual process next week.

blocks.title: Keep a before and after pair
blocks.text: Save one weak draft next to its edited version in the same Google Doc. After a few weeks, that pair shows which defaults keep coming back. It also teaches new teammates faster than a long guide.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. It lives in the notch, listens and looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut, and answers out loud. For this problem, it can draft text and type it into the app you are working in. Dictation can speak your first rough version at the cursor. It cannot know your voice without the card and samples you give it. It does not post, send, or click for you, so the review step stays with you.

Two features matter most here. Snippets, a personal dictionary, and clipboard slots keep approved wording the same from draft to draft. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Some writers find that speaking gives a looser first draft. Try it on one post and compare the result with your typed draft.

If you are unsure where a control lives, ask Lazur to walk you through it. Lazur guides you one click at a time and waits for each click, so you learn the path yourself. For a quick location, ask it to point. It draws a circle and a label around the control on your screen.
Edge cases: regulated work, shared drafts, and AI checks

If you work in law, nursing, or accounting, follow your employer's rules on client or patient data before you paste anything into a prompt. Remove names, account numbers, and case details from samples. Lazur sends audio and the screenshot to AI providers to answer them, and they are not stored. Your employer's policy still decides what you may share.

blocks.title: Check before you paste
blocks.text: Do not paste client, patient, or account details into a prompt unless your employer's policy allows it. When in doubt, write a fake sample with the same structure and use that instead.

Some teams ask AI to check AI. Ahrefs found that 29% of AI users now ask AI to check AI content, up from 14% the year before. Manual self-checking was still the most common method. A second model can catch some problems, but it cannot approve your claims. Keep a person on facts.

If your team drafts in Microsoft Word, Microsoft's Copilot in Word page advises including reference documents and the required writing style to help produce a first draft in minutes. The page does not mention Mac or brand voice. Test that approach on one sample before you rely on it.
Mistakes that bring the drift back

items: Writing a voice card of adjectives only, with no samples behind it.
Using the same generic prompt for every channel, from email to social.
Letting a Writing Tools rewrite remove the personality from a draft.
Accepting numbers and claims without checking the source.
Skipping the review because the draft reads smoothly.
Never updating the card after the edits teach you something new.

blocks.text: What to do next

Start small. Pick one asset type, such as a launch email or a short social post, and run this routine for one week. Keep the card and samples in one Google Doc so every drafter uses the same version. If your team also reviews copy in Google Docs, the [Google Docs guide for marketers](/for/marketers/google-docs) covers review and comment habits.

Judge the result by edit time and reader feedback, not by how fast the first draft appeared. A draft that takes longer to fix than to write does not save time. If you want to try the voice assistant, the [download page](/download) has the Mac app, and [pricing](/pricing) lists the plans.

faq.question: Can AI write marketing copy in my brand voice on its own?
faq.answer: Not reliably. Without samples, the model falls back to a generic middle voice. Give it a voice card and three to five real samples, then review every draft against them.

faq.question: How many examples should I give an AI for tone?
faq.answer: Anthropic's prompting guide suggests three to five examples for best results, chosen to match the use case and cover different cases. Start with three. Add another only when the output misses a specific pattern.

faq.question: Does Apple Writing Tools match my brand voice?
faq.answer: Not by itself. Writing Tools offers Friendly, Professional, and Concise rewrites, plus Proofread. Those move text toward a general tone. Use them to tighten copy you already drafted in your voice. Availability depends on Apple Intelligence support in your language and region.

faq.question: Do I need to buy a tool to fix AI drift?
faq.answer: No. A voice card, a sample set, a banned words list, and a checklist cost nothing. A paid tool might save some pasting, but it does not replace the review step.

faq.question: How often should I review AI drafts before publishing?
faq.answer: Review every draft before it goes out. Ahrefs' 2026 survey found that 66% of marketers trust AI content only after a human reviews it first, and 2.7% trust it with no review at all.

faq.question: Can I put client or patient details into an AI prompt?
faq.answer: Follow your employer's rules first. If you work in law, nursing, or accounting, client or patient data may be restricted. Strip identifying details from samples unless your policy allows them. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut.

faq.question: Why does my AI copy still sound generic with a brand guide?
faq.answer: Guides written as adjectives stay vague, and models struggle to imitate informal, nuanced voices. Samples and a banned list give more signal. Expect to do the final pass by hand.

faq.question: Does Lazur write in my voice?
faq.answer: Lazur drafts and types text using the voice card and samples you paste into the request. It does not post, send, or click for you, so you check the draft before it goes anywhere.

costs.title: Editing time you did not plan for
costs.text: A draft that is mostly right still needs a full read. You rewrite template-like sentences, fix claims, and check tone. The minutes you save on the first draft can return as edit time if the voice is off. Track edit time for one asset type for a week and compare it with your old process.

costs.text: Ahrefs' 2026 survey found that 56% of AI users say human-written content is better quality than their AI content, and 23% say it is way better. Readers may not name the difference, but they feel it in the first line.

costs.title: Trust that depends on a person
costs.text: Only 2.7% of respondents trust AI content with no review at all. If your team publishes AI copy without a check, your process sits outside the norm the survey describes. That matters when a reviewer asks why a post sounds different from the rest.

costs.title: Workload that already feels heavy
costs.text: CMI's February 2026 survey of 644 full-time marketers found that 59% say their workload feels overwhelming, and 76% say they do the work of more than one job. The survey is about general workload. A draft that needs heavy rewriting can add work instead of cutting it.

costs.title: Claims you never approved
costs.text: Brand voice is not only tone. Generic copy can drift into promises and numbers that nobody signed off on. A Shorthand VP quoted in Ahrefs' article says AI copy can make a brand sound like every other content platform, so her team keeps personality-heavy copy human-written.

causes.title: Assistant framing leaks into your message

Cornell reports that people using it were twice as likely to write a paragraph agreeing with the assistant. A default slant in a tool can become your slant.

causes.title: Shared prompts produce look-alike copy
causes.text: Doshi and Hauser's dataset of 293 participants found that AI-enabled stories were more similar to each other than stories by humans alone. If your team uses one generic prompt, the posts will rhyme. The fix is to give each drafter the same specific samples, not the same generic instruction.

causes.title: Informal voices are hard to copy
causes.text: Wang and colleagues tested more than 40,000 generations per model across writing from more than 400 real authors. Models did better with structured formats like news and email. They struggled with nuanced, informal blogs and forums, which is where many brand voices live.

causes.title: Vague prompts ask for vague output
causes.text: A prompt that says make it on brand gives the model nothing to match. Anthropic's guide says examples are among the most reliable ways to steer tone. Without examples, the model guesses, and the guess tends toward the middle.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Write the voice card
plan.text: Draft one page with five traits, a counter-example for each, your usual opener and closer, and your banned words. Keep it in one Google Doc and share the link with every drafter.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Collect three to five samples
plan.text: Pull past posts, emails, and help articles that you think sound like the brand. Pick a mix of formats. Remove client names, account numbers, and any detail your employer's policy restricts.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Draft one asset type in steps
plan.text: Ask for three openers, pick one, then ask for the body. Log the minutes you spend editing. Do not skip the log, because it is your only proof that the routine saves time.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Run the checklist and update the list
plan.text: Search for banned words, check every number against a source, and read the draft aloud. Add each word you deleted to the banned list, and note any claim that needed a source.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Run the blind test and review
plan.text: Give two colleagues the draft and a published post without labels. Ask which sounds more like the brand. Update the voice card with their reasons, and compare this week's edit minutes with your usual process.
